author: historian-agent:mig-1
title: Bantu expansion
summary: Speakers of Bantu languages spread from the Nigeria-Cameroon borderlands across central, eastern and southern Africa over about 4,000 years. Sources agree on the homeland but differ on timing and routes, and some argue for a pause or collapse in the rainforest around 400-600 CE followed by renewed settlement.

uncertainty.note: Years are 1950 minus the age, or calendar years. Start: "starting ~4000 years ago" (Seidensticker et al. 2021); OpenStax gives 3000-2000 BCE (start_minus 950). Route dates are the contested part: OpenStax places the eastern stream in the Great Lakes about 1500 BCE, the newsletter gives the Urewe tradition from about 600 BC, and Urewe ware as a 2nd-5th century CE find. The waypoints follow the eastern stream only; a western stream through Kinshasa and Angola is described in the sources but not shown.

as_recorded.value: Bantu spread starting ~4000 years ago from the Nigeria-Cameroon border; Congo rainforest reached around 2700 years ago
Expansion likely began between 3000 and 2000 BCE; eastern stream in the Great Lakes around 1500 BCE
Urewe tradition began around 600 BC; Kwale wares appear in KwaZulu-Natal 200-300 CE
Kwale ware, an offshoot of Urewe ware, dates to around the third century

when.display: c. 2000 BCE to 300 CE (routes and dates debated)

where.modern_name: Shum Laka rock shelter, Northwest Region, Cameroon (proxy for the Nigeria-Cameroon border homeland)
where.historical_name: Western Central Africa at the southern edge of the Sahara-era wet phase; no states or recorded place names

waypoints.label: Nigeria-Cameroon borderland, the Bantu homeland. Point is Shum Laka, a rock shelter the newsletter places within the homeland; the homeland is a region, not a site.
Congo rainforest, the first ecozone reached by ancestral Bantu speakers. Point is the Congo Basin centre; the region is very large.

waypoints.date: began around 600 BC (Urewe tradition; African History Extra). Contested: OpenStax gives the Great Lakes about 1500 BCE, Urewe ware 2nd-5th century CE
waypoints.label: Urewe, Lake Victoria basin, Kenya: type site of the Great Lakes Early Iron Age tradition.

waypoints.date: around the third century (Kwale ware, OpenStax)
waypoints.label: Kwale County, Kenyan coast: type area of Kwale ware, an offshoot of Urewe ware; the newsletter dates Kwale/Matola ceramics to the 2nd century CE.

waypoints.date: 200-300 CE (Kwale wares in KwaZulu-Natal, African History Extra)
waypoints.label: KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa: Kwale ware appears 200-300 CE. Point is the province centre; individual sites are not named in the source.

importance.justification: One of the largest human migrations, spreading Bantu languages and, over time, farming and ironworking across much of the continent.

reviewer_note: Least sure: Great Lakes date (600 BC vs 1500 BCE vs 2nd-5th century CE); rainforest point is a basin centroid; KwaZulu-Natal and Kwale are regional proxies, not sites; Shum Laka stands for the homeland; the newsletter source is class other and should be replaced by an academic review.

beats.caption: Bantu-speaking communities begin to spread from the borderlands of Nigeria and Cameroon, around 4,000 years ago on the genetic and linguistic estimate.
Speakers reach the Congo rainforest around 2,700 years ago; the Urewe tradition appears near Lake Victoria, with dates debated.
Kwale wares reach the Kenyan coast and KwaZulu-Natal in the early centuries CE, carrying Bantu languages and farming to southern Africa.
